solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Nice socialist relatives (7)

blocks.note: a red is a socialist or communist, from the red flag

annotation.surface: A pleasant left-wing family, sketched in three words.
annotation.walkthrough: "Nice" at the start tempts you toward the French city, but it only means kind here.
annotation.definitionFit: Used as a plural noun, kindred means your family or kin, the people related to you by blood.

entries.clue: Joint leader is an idiot (11)

blocks.note: a knuckle is a finger joint

annotation.surface: A complaint that whoever runs a joint venture, or a dodgy bar, is a fool.
annotation.walkthrough: "Joint leader" reads as one person at the top of a shared enterprise; split it into two words to get the body part and the boss.
annotation.definitionFit: Chiefly American slang, calling someone thick-headed, as if their head were solid bone like a knuckle.

entries.clue: Chat about setter being better dressed (7)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so the word for chat goes around the setter

blocks.note: natter = chat, a British word for idle talk
the setter refers to themself as I

annotation.surface: A gossip about the crossword setter's smarter wardrobe.
annotation.walkthrough: NATTER opens after its second T to take I. "Setter" meaning I (or ME) is a standing convention.
annotation.definitionFit: Natty is an informal word for smart and neat in dress, and the comparative is the sense here.

entries.clue: Hurls ripe bananas in supremo’s office (9)

indicatorNotes.bananas: bananas is slang for crazy, and letters that go crazy lose their order

annotation.surface: Someone flings overripe bananas around the boss's office.
annotation.walkthrough: "Ripe bananas" reads as fruit, but "bananas" is the instruction and "ripe" is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: The office of a ruler, the post a supremo holds; office is the position, not the room.

entries.clue: Endlessly debate athletic event (6)

indicatorNotes.Endlessly: without an end, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: a seven-letter verb for debate, less its last letter

annotation.surface: A complaint about an argument that drags on over a sports fixture.
annotation.walkthrough: DISCUSS loses its final S. "Endlessly" looks like an adverb for a tedious debate, but it cuts the last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Named by its implement: the discus throw is the field event in which the heavy disc is hurled.

entries.clue: Piece of information concealed by chief actors (4)

indicatorNotes.concealed by: something concealed by other words sits inside them, so the answer is tucked into the next words

annotation.surface: A secret the lead actors are keeping back.
annotation.walkthrough: The letters bridge the gap between the two words: the last letter of chief and the start of actors.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a single item of knowledge or data, a detail known to be true.

entries.clue: Bit of fish finger, half gone (3)

indicatorNotes.half gone: if half of the word is gone, only its first half is left

blocks.note: a deletion: keep the first three of its six letters, the second half gone

annotation.surface: Someone has eaten half a fish finger.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fish finger" reads as one breaded snack, but "fish" belongs to the definition and "finger" is the word to cut; a fish finger is a fish stick.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by part: the fin is the bit of a fish it swims and steers with.

entries.clue: Hop bud, pickled (5)

blocks.note: a verb: to skip or leap about playfully
the flower bud of a Mediterranean shrub, preserved in brine or vinegar

annotation.surface: A brewer's shopping note: hop buds, pickled.
annotation.walkthrough: "Hop" and "bud" both push you toward beer-making, but "hop" is the jump, not the plant.
annotation.definitionFit: Two unrelated words share the spelling: the frisky leap, from Latin for goat, and the pickled bud used in cooking.

entries.clue: Left after naked auntie — or before? (5)

indicatorNotes.naked: a naked word is stripped of its covering, its outer letters
indicatorNotes.after: L is left after the rest, so it is placed at the end

blocks.note: AUNTIE without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A startled observer tries to work out whether they left after or before the naked aunt appeared.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a loose definition: the word marks the point up to which something lasts, so it sits close to before.
annotation.definitionFit: "Don't eat till six" and "don't eat before six" say the same, so the preposition and before overlap in sense.

entries.clue: Spades and excavation in play area (7)

blocks.note: a pit is a hole dug out

annotation.surface: Children digging with spades in the playground.
annotation.walkthrough: The spades look like toy shovels, but here they are the card suit giving S; a sandpit is the British word for a sandbox.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: a shallow pit of sand where children dig and play.

entries.clue: Record means something important to tailor (4,7)

blocks.note: a measure is a means to an end, a step taken

annotation.surface: A claim that a record means a lot to a tailor.
annotation.walkthrough: "Means" reads as a verb but is a noun, a measure; "tailor" is the noun too, not the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by use: the flexible marked tape a tailor takes body measurements with.

entries.clue: Caught shy fish (3)

indicatorNotes.Caught: a sound you caught is one you heard, so the next word is said aloud

blocks.note: coy = shy, and the fish is pronounced the same

annotation.surface: An angler lands a timid fish.
annotation.walkthrough: "Caught" suggests a fishing catch, or C in cricket, but here it means heard.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the ornamental carp kept in garden ponds.

entries.clue: Going to the bar and back? (5,4)

annotation.definition: Going to the bar and back?

blocks.note: the surface pushes a pub visit; the setter means fetching drinks for your whole group
the return leg makes it a journey out and home again

annotation.surface: Heading to the pub counter and returning.
annotation.walkthrough: Buying a round means fetching drinks for your whole group from the bar, a British pub custom, so the trip there and back is round in two senses.
annotation.definitionFit: The travel phrase for an outward journey plus the return, borrowed here for a trip to fetch a round.

entries.clue: Finally reprimanded for one’s manners in roads (9)

indicatorNotes.Finally: finally points to what comes at the end, here the last letter of each of the next two words

blocks.note: last letters of reprimandeD and foR

annotation.surface: Someone has at last been told off for their behaviour on the roads.
annotation.walkthrough: "One's" is read as "one has", giving I'VE. The definition is roads leading in, from the street to a house.
annotation.definitionFit: Read cryptically: private tracks that lead in from the street to a house or garage, so roads in.

entries.clue: They are mostly rough and ribald (6)

indicatorNotes.mostly: mostly means not all, so the phrase loses its last letter
indicatorNotes.rough: something roughed up is disordered, so the letters are shaken up

blocks.note: THEY ARE without its final E

annotation.surface: A description of some coarse, bawdy people.
annotation.walkthrough: "Rough and ribald" reads as a pair of adjectives, but "rough" is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Earthy humour is frank about bodily things, crude in the way ribald jokes are.

entries.clue: Stupid amount of money for dumplings (3,3)

annotation.surface: A grumble about the silly price of some dumplings.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface prices the food; split it and the insult and the amount are the two halves.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Cantonese small dishes, above all steamed dumplings, served with tea.

entries.clue: Japanese scoff and hiss — I am out of order (7)

indicatorNotes.out of order: letters out of order are not in their proper sequence, so rearrange them

annotation.surface: A diner wolfs down Japanese food and hisses, then apologises for bad manners.
annotation.walkthrough: "Scoff" is British slang for food as a noun, not the verb to eat greedily or to mock.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: thin slices of raw fish, a Japanese dish, and scoff is slang for food.

entries.clue: Force you to put on frock (6)

indicatorNotes.to put on: you put on a frock by getting inside it, so U goes inside the dress

blocks.note: U sounds like you, as in text speak

annotation.surface: Being made to wear a dress.
annotation.walkthrough: DRESS opens after the D to take U. The surface is apt: being forced into a frock is duress.
annotation.definitionFit: A legal and everyday synonym: threats or pressure used to make someone act against their will.

entries.clue: Bust put nearer entrance (9)

indicatorNotes.Bust: bust means broken, and broken letters are put back together in a new order

annotation.surface: An instruction to move a sculpted bust closer to the doorway.
annotation.walkthrough: "Entrance" looks like a doorway, but read it as en-TRANCE, the verb to delight; "Bust" is broken, not a statue.
annotation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to hold someone spellbound with delight, one by rapture, the other by trance.

entries.clue: Drove fast car over England’s borders (5)

indicatorNotes.over: turned over, so it reads upward in a down clue
indicatorNotes.borders: a country's borders are its edges, so take the first and last letters

blocks.note: first and last letters of EnglanD

annotation.surface: Someone sped a car across the English border.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fast car" reads as one phrase, but "fast" belongs to the definition and "car" alone is reversed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to race a car is to drive it at speed.

entries.clue: Reportedly go out with marine (3)

annotation.definitionNote: marine is an adjective; SEA serves as one only before a noun, as in sea creatures

indicatorNotes.Reportedly: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the word is heard, not seen

blocks.note: to see someone is to go out with them, date them

annotation.surface: Gossip that someone is dating a soldier from the Marines.
annotation.walkthrough: "Marine" reads as a person to date, but it is the adjective, as in marine life.
annotation.definitionFit: The noun used attributively: sea life and marine life are the same thing, from Latin mare, sea.

entries.clue: Downturn in trade after last month (7)

indicatorNotes.after: after means following, so the trade word follows the month

blocks.note: DEC, December, is the last month of the year
one's line is one's trade, line of work

annotation.surface: A business report of falling sales since last month.
annotation.walkthrough: "Last month" reads as the previous month, but it is December, the final month of the year.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from economics: a fall in activity or value, a slump.

entries.clue: Trendy new pub (3)

blocks.note: in = fashionable, as in the in thing

annotation.surface: A fashionable new bar has opened.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one opening; split it into two chunks and both adjectives give letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: an old-fashioned name for a pub, especially one that once offered rooms.

entries.clue: See you and Mike run regularly (5)

indicatorNotes.regularly: at regular intervals, so take every other letter

blocks.note: the count carries on: m I k E

annotation.surface: Saying goodbye to Mike as he sets off on his jog.
annotation.walkthrough: Mike looks like a friend's name; it is only there for its letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A French farewell borrowed into English, used as a parting word just as see you is.

entries.clue: Opening of exclusive retreat in paradise (4)

indicatorNotes.Opening of: a word's opening is its start, so take its first letter

blocks.note: a den is a private retreat

annotation.surface: An advert for a luxury holiday resort in a tropical paradise.
annotation.walkthrough: "Opening" sounds like a launch of the resort; it only takes the first letter of the next word.
annotation.definitionFit: The biblical garden of Genesis, used by extension for any place of perfect happiness.

entries.clue: Famous chapel is set in Barking (7)

indicatorNotes.Barking: barking is British slang for mad, and mad letters are scrambled

annotation.surface: A claim that a famous chapel stands in Barking, a district of east London.
annotation.walkthrough: Barking is a place in London, and "barking" is British slang for mad; here it is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Vatican chapel famed for Michelangelo's ceiling.
